title: Wireless telegraphy: Hertzian waves to Marconi transatlantic signaling amid rival radio routes
pressure: Maxwellian waves had to become a communication system with reproducible generation/detection, antennas/grounding/tuning, enough range, signal discrimination, operations and institutional support. Long range also tested propagation assumptions that short demonstrations could not settle.
preExistingWorldModel: Hertz generated/detected electromagnetic waves in the late 1880s as physics evidence, not a ready service. Coherer-like detectors and antenna work supplied components Marconi integrated into signaling; Fessenden pursued materially different continuous-wave/voice paths.
candidateRoutes: retain cable/telegraph for high-reliability long distance
observationsAndInstruments: Hertz's experiments established wave behavior consistent with Maxwellian electromagnetism.
Marconi combined spark transmitter, detector, antenna/ground and procedures, patented in Britain and formed a company in the late 1890s.
Range rose from local tests to maritime links and the reported 1901 Newfoundland transatlantic reception.
The 1901 event was a weak one-way signal rather than a mature transatlantic commercial channel; later station/tuning/receiver work remained.
Fessenden pursued continuous-wave/radiotelephone approaches, showing wireless was an architecture family rather than one route.
decisiveTests: Laboratory waves had to carry intentionally encoded signals outdoors.
Range claims had to survive different geography/weather/equipment conditions.
Weak transatlantic reception had to be separated from durable two-way commercial service.
As stations multiplied, selectivity/interference became tests that transmitter power alone could not solve.
technicalOrScientificTransition: A physics phenomenon became communications infrastructure through system integration. Each scale increase changed the bottleneck: existence of waves → detection → range → selectivity/interference → operations/regulation.
rivalsAndFailures: Wired/submarine telegraph remained more reliable on many routes.
1901 long-range reception was informative but not service closure.
Fessenden continuous-wave routes targeted capabilities spark systems handled poorly.
High power without selectivity caused interference as stations multiplied.
Grand wireless visions such as Wardenclyffe could outrun technical-financial closure.
diffusionAndScaling: Ship/shore wireless spread rapidly; long-distance stations expanded; shared-spectrum coordination became an international problem.
standardsAndInstitutions: Wireless firms, navies, shipping companies and states held distinct authority; later conventions constrained call signs/distress/operating practice.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Interference and refusal to relay competitors' traffic created shared-resource/safety externalities.
secondOrderEffects: Wireless became substrate for broadcasting, mobile radio, radar and radio science.
sourceNativeSummary: Wireless is a scale ladder, not one invention: Hertz made waves observable, Marconi integrated signaling, 1901 challenged range assumptions without closing service, and rival continuous-wave plus interference pressures changed the architecture again.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: How should component/integration credit be distributed among Hertz, Branly, Lodge, Popov, Marconi and others?
What evidence best separates the informational value of 1901 reception from later service reliability?
